name: Verne Leagues
lines: Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea
Jules Verne · Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea (1870), the whole book, Parts One and Two

1866: a monster is sinking ships. Professor Aronnax, his servant Conseil and Ned Land the harpooner sail to hunt it on the frigate Abraham Lincoln, and find Captain Nemo instead. Ten months under the seas of the world aboard the Nautilus, every chapter as Verne wrote it: about five hours and more at your own pace.
the frigate Abraham Lincoln, at her pier on the quay
Not that way: turn to face it first. The light shows where.
Professor Aronnax's rooms, New York
Out onto the quay of the Voyages: Brooklyn pier for today, and the frigate alongside.
🏨 Professor Aronnax's rooms, New York, March 1867. A parlour heaped with the crates of his six months in Nebraska; the newspapers of two continents on the desk.
The newspapers on the desk
read what the world says of the monster
📰 The newspapers, March 1867 The New York Herald, the Times of London, the Journal des Débats: every one of them has the monster.
In every place of great resort the monster was the fashion.
They sang of it in the cafés, mocked it in the papers, and represented it on the stage.
The Nebraska collection
look at the crates
🦬 The Nebraska collection Six months of mineralogy, botany and zoology from the badlands of Nebraska, waiting for the ship to Paris.
After six months in Nebraska, I arrived in New York towards the end of March, laden with a precious collection.
see what Conseil is packing
🧳 Shirts, instruments, the professor's notebooks; and on top, carefully, the case of preserved specimens Conseil has classified himself.
The door to the street
go down to Brooklyn pier
the frigate Abraham Lincoln
Back down the gangway onto the quay.
⚓ The Abraham Lincoln. A frigate of great speed, United States Navy, under Commander Farragut: three masts, a tall funnel, every gun loaded, every man looking out to sea.
The shrouds of the mainmast
climb to the main top
🔭 The main top. Twenty-two metres over the deck, the whole sea round you. Every man aboard would give a year's pay to be the first to see the monster.
The way down the shrouds
climb down to the deck
The engine-room skylight
listen to the engines
🔥 Below, the stokers feed the furnaces; the high-pressure engines thud.
Under this the Abraham Lincoln attained the mean speed of nearly eighteen knots and a third an hour
The long gun on the forecastle
💥 A breech-loading gun, the newest the arsenals had; it throws a shell of four kilos nine miles.
Ned Land's harpoons
look at the harpoons
🔱 Five harpoons and the lines coiled in their tubs. Ned Land's own is the long one, its iron worn bright.
The frigate's wheel
look at the compass
🧭 The binnacle compass swings and settles: the frigate's course is set for the North Pacific, where the monster was last seen.
The commander's charts
look at the charts
🗺️ Farragut's charts of the Pacific, the monster's sightings marked in red ink, each with its date.
Cabin No. 2, the professor's
go into your cabin
🛏️ A cabin aft, opening on the wardroom; Conseil has stowed the trunks under the bunk.
go back down to the quay
the Nautilus: the cabins
Back on the jetty in the sea cave.

🌊 The Nautilus, the cabins. A passage of riveted plate lit by electric globes: the cells, the professor's room, Captain Nemo's room, the galley and the crew's quarters; the iron stair up to the platform.
The cell's iron walls
🔩 Sheet-iron, bolted, without a seam you could get a nail into. No window. A door with no handle on this side.
🛏️ A room fit for a guest: a bed, a dressing-table, a desk, and close by, the iron hull; beyond it, the sea.
Ned and Conseil's cabin
🛏️ Two bunks. Ned Land's harpoon leans in the corner (Nemo lets him keep it); Conseil's notebook of classifications lies open on the other.
The iron stair to the platform
go up onto the platform
The instruments in Captain Nemo's room
look at the instruments
🧭 The instruments Thermometer, barometer, hygrometer, storm-glass, compass, sextant, chronometers, and the manometer that tells by the pressure of the water how deep she is.
"These are the usual nautical instruments,"
here are the contrivances required for the navigation of the Nautilus.
The portraits on Nemo's wall
look at the portraits

🖼️ The portraits Engravings of the great men who gave their lives for the freedom of their people: Kosciusko, Botzaris, O'Connell, Washington, Manin, Lincoln, and John Brown. And over the bed, a small portrait of a young woman and two little children.
The galley's still
Then a door opened into a kitchen nine feet long, situated between the large store-rooms.
Beside it, the still that boils sea-water and gives fresh water to drink.
🛁 A bath-room, with hot and cold taps. Everything aboard, Nemo says, is done by electricity.
The ladder to the dinghy
look up the ladder
🚣 The ladder climbs through a manhole into the dinghy, fitted into a recess of the hull. Both hatches close tight: the boat leaves the Nautilus, under the sea or on it.
The ladder to the salon
go up to the library and the salon
The crew's quarters
🛌 Hammocks for twenty men, sea chests between. The crew speak among themselves a language no one aboard but they understands.
📦 Casks of preserved fish, sea-weed flour, sugar from the sea-wrack, oil, the sodium in sealed jars.
the Nautilus, on the surface
🌊 The platform of the Nautilus. Her back of riveted iron, two or three feet out of the sea; the lantern's cage forward, the pilot's cage aft of it; the hatch open behind you.
go down into the Nautilus
The dinghy, drawn up on the beach
row back to the Nautilus
row ashore to Gilboa
🏝️ Gilboa. White sand, coral at the water's edge, and behind it the forest climbing the hills:
the Island of Gilboa
the hollow volcano
🌋 Inside the volcano. A lake of sea-water ringed by black walls a hundred metres high, open to the sky at the top. The Nautilus lies at a quay of basalt. Along the walls, the crew are mining coal.
Here, in their diving-dresses, pick axe and shovel in hand, my men extract the coal, which I do not even ask from the mines of the earth.
The seam runs black and shining through the lava; the crew cut it and wheel it to the quay.
ask what is made here
⚗️ The coal heats the furnaces; the furnaces break down the salt of the sea; out of it comes sodium, and the sodium makes the Nautilus's electricity.
The ledge high in the crater
🌋 Far below, the lake and the Nautilus, small as a fish; high above, the round of sky. The walls are black lava, streaked with sulphur.
The Nautilus, at the basalt quay
🧊 Under the ice. Walls of ice above, below, on every side. The Nautilus hangs in the middle of it, her lantern lighting the blue. The crew go out in the diving dress with picks.
The diving hatch of the Nautilus
a fisherman's hut, the Lofoten Isles
Out onto the mole by the lighthouse, the sea calm.
🏠 A fisherman's hut on the Lofoten Isles, off Norway. Plank walls, a stove, nets drying; out of the window, the grey northern sea.
The window over the sea
🌊 Grey sea, grey sky, the far shore of the mainland. Somewhere out there, the Maelstrom, quiet now with the turn of the tide.
The door of the hut
The wrecks of Vanikoro
look at the wrecks

⚓ Vanikoro, 1788 The ribs of two frigates under the coral: cannon, anchors, a bronze bell. The Boussole and the Astrolabe of the Count de La Pérouse, sent round the world by King Louis XVI, were lost here in a hurricane in 1788. Nobody knew where, until Dumont d'Urville found these in 1828.
The great oyster in the grotto
look at the oyster
🦪 A tridacna more than two metres across, its shell half open; inside, on the folds of its mantle, a pearl the size of a coconut. Captain Nemo will not take it. He lets it grow.

Ned Land, the Canadian harpooner, 'the prince of harpooners', about forty, tall, strong, grave, quick to anger; from Quebec, speaks French and English; a whaler who believes only what he has seen. In 1867-68 he is aboard the frigate Abraham Lincoln and then, a prisoner, aboard the Nautilus, where all he wants is to escape.

Conseil, Professor Aronnax's servant, a Flemish lad of thirty, devoted, calm in every danger, who speaks to his master in the third person ('if master pleases') and classifies every creature by branch, class, order, family, genus and species.

Captain Nemo, commander of the Nautilus, 1867-68: a man of science and of great sorrow, who has broken with the land and all its laws. Proud, courteous, cold, generous to the oppressed; you never learn his country or his past. Speak as he does in Verne's book.
Professor Pierre Aronnax of the Museum of Natural History in Paris, the narrator of the book: a naturalist, curious, honest, torn between wonder at the Nautilus and longing for freedom.
A page of the Shipping Gazette, 1867
1866 and 1867: something enormous in the seas
A clerk of the Cunard Line
A shipping clerk of the Cunard Line in New York, 1867, full of the news of the Scotia, struck by something in mid-Atlantic. Talkative, sure it is a monster.
You've heard about the Scotia? Struck in the open sea, sir, by something nobody saw.
An old whaling captain
An old whaling captain on the New York quays, 1867, who has hunted whales thirty years and has never seen anything like what the log-books report. Gruff, honest.
Thirty years I've hunted whales. Never one three hundred feet long.
A clerk of the Cunard Line has the latest news. Ask him about the Scotia.
Mid-Atlantic, a fine sea, the passengers at lunch.

At seventeen minutes past four in the afternoon, whilst the passengers were assembled at lunch in the great saloon, a slight shock was felt on the hull of the Scotia, on her quarter, a little aft of the port-paddle.
When they put her in dry dock, there in her iron hull was a hole.
▶ 'What kind of hole?'
🔺 The Scotia's wound
The engineers could hardly believe it: two yards and a half below the water-line, a clean rent in two inches of iron. What shape was it?
A ragged split, like a rock would make
A regular isosceles triangle
A round hole, like a cannon ball
A rock tears and crumples. This was clean.
No gun fired at the Scotia.
at two yards and a half below water-mark was a regular rent, in the form of an isosceles triangle.
An old whaling captain on the quay has read every log-book. Ask him what the ships have seen.

July 1866, the Governor Higginson, off Australia: a 'moving sandbank' spouting water a hundred and fifty feet high. Days later, the Christopher Columbus, in the Pacific. Then the Helvetia and the Shannon, in the Atlantic, two thousand miles away:

Fifteen days later, two thousand miles farther off, the Helvetia, of the Compagnie-Nationale, and the Shannon, of the Royal Mail Steamship Company, sailing to windward in that portion of the Atlantic lying between the United States and Europe, respectively signalled the monster to each other

The Shannon and the Helvetia, side by side, measured it against their own hulls: they said it was more than 350 English feet long. The largest whales ever measured were about a third of that. If it was a whale...
Three hundred and fifty feet is no ordinary whale.
Two ships' crews, two thousand miles from the first sighting, saw the same thing.
If it was a whale, it surpassed in size all those hitherto classified in science.
A page of the Shipping Gazette
A page of the Shipping Gazette has blown along the quay. Pick it up: every sinking of the year is in it, and every one 'put down to the monster'.
📰 The monster in the fashion
They sang of it in the cafés, laughed at it in the papers, played it on the stage. And then the Scotia: after that, nobody laughed.
From this moment all unlucky casualties which could not be otherwise accounted for were put down to the monster.
Stand at the quay's edge by the frigate and look out over the harbour, where the sea runs out to the ocean.
Professor Aronnax's rooms in New York, spring 1867
A reporter of the New York Herald
A reporter of the New York Herald, 1867, who wants Professor Aronnax of the Paris Museum to say, in print, what the monster is. Eager, quick, a notebook in hand.
Professor! One word for the Herald: what is the thing? A reef? A ship? A beast?
Ah, you have come at a lively moment. Everyone wants my opinion on this monster.
Look at the newspapers on Professor Aronnax's desk: every one of them is full of the monster.
Look at the crates from Nebraska, the professor's six months of work, waiting for the ship home to Paris.
Speak with Professor Aronnax, of the Paris Museum. He is the one telling this story.
At the period when these events took place, I had just returned from a scientific research in the disagreeable territory of Nebraska, in the United States.

I am Assistant Professor in the Museum of Natural History in Paris, and the newspapers have found me out. I wrote a book, The Mysteries of the Great Submarine Grounds. So now they want me to say what this thing is.'
The reporter of the New York Herald wants the professor's answer for tomorrow's paper. Hear the two sides.

There remained, then, only two possible solutions of the question, which created two distinct parties: on one side, those who were for a monster of colossal strength; on the other, those who were for a submarine vessel of enormous motive power.
▶ What does the professor say?
🦄 The professor's answer
Aronnax reasons it out: no reef moves; no government has such a ship. It must be an animal, and one that can drive a horn through iron. Which of the sea's creatures is armed with a long ivory sword?
The narwhal, the unicorn of the sea
The sperm whale has teeth, but no sword.
A squid has arms and a beak, no sword.
The common narwhal, or unicorn of the sea, often attains a length of sixty feet.
Make it ten times stronger and larger, Aronnax writes, and you have the monster.
A letter has just come. It lies on the desk, under the newspapers. Open it.
Commander Farragut has a cabin at your disposal.
The frigate sails from Brooklyn pier in three hours.
I Form My Resolution
